clue.text: Idyllic clue from Barrie, anglicized as of right

definitions.text: Idyllic clue from Barrie, anglicized as of right

parts.words: Idyllic clue from Barrie, anglicized as of right
parts.note: J M Barrie wrote Auld Licht Idylls; put the Scots title words into standard English and you get the legal term for windows enjoying light by long-established right

explanation.surface: A hint taken from a Barrie idyll, put into English, appears to describe a legal entitlement.
explanation.walkthrough: Barrie's book Auld Licht Idylls is about the 'Old Light' Scottish sect; in English 'auld licht' becomes 'ancient light', which in English law is a window whose light a neighbour may not block, enjoyed as of right.
explanation.definitionFit: In English property law the phrase names windows that have acquired a prescriptive right to daylight after twenty years' use.

clue.text: War picture in the modern manner ?

definitions.text: War picture in the modern manner ?

parts.words: War picture in the modern manner
parts.note: a 'war picture' could be a battle painting, but read as 'battle' plus 'painting' it names the splashy abstract style of Jackson Pollock

explanation.surface: Someone describes a battle scene done in a contemporary style.
explanation.walkthrough: Action means fighting, so a war picture is literally an action painting; the term actually names the mid-century style of dripping and flinging paint.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a modern abstract technique where paint is dripped or hurled onto the canvas, as Pollock did.

clue.text: Just the stuff for junketing

parts.note: junketing sounds like partying, but junket is also a sweet dish of set milk, which is made from the solid part of soured milk

explanation.surface: Someone recommends supplies for a jolly outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junketing' means feasting or merrymaking, but a junket is a dessert of milk set with rennet, so the stuff it needs is the thickened milk solids.
explanation.definitionFit: Curdled milk solids are what a junket, a rennet-set milk pudding, consists of.

clue.text: Last in sees to these necessities

indicators.note: the letters of the first three words are turned into these, the words that follow, so they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The one who comes in last attends to the basic requirements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sees to' looks like a phrase meaning attends to, but 'sees' is part of the anagram fodder, and 'to these' asks for LASTINSEES to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean the things that are indispensable or absolutely required.

clue.text: Hornblower's habitat ?

parts.note: Hornblower suggests C S Forester's naval hero, but a horn blower toots, and a place named for that action is a south London district

explanation.surface: Someone asks where Captain Hornblower might live.
explanation.walkthrough: A horn-blower is one who is always tooting, and TOOTING is a district of south London, so it is jokily made the tooter's home ground.
explanation.definitionFit: The south London district's name reads as the present participle of the verb for sounding a horn.

clue.text: Help coming up among locals for the brave fellows

indicators.note: one piece sits among the letters of the other, so it goes inside

parts.note: a local is a British pub, an inn

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: help means aid

explanation.surface: Assistance arrives among the local people for some courageous men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' reverses AID to DIA, which goes 'among' INNS. A 'local' is the British word for one's neighbourhood pub; 'braves' are Native American warriors.
explanation.definitionFit: Native American warriors were traditionally called braves in older adventure writing.

clue.text: Merriment in the depression?

definitions.meaning: laughter, the sound of people laughing
a sunken ditch with a wall on one side, used as an invisible boundary in landscaped gardens

explanation.surface: Someone asks if there can be jollity during a low period.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a sunk fence: a ditch that keeps livestock out of a garden without blocking the view, common on English country estates.
explanation.definitionFit: Laughter is written as a repeated laughing syllable, and a sunk fence in landscape gardening bears the same name.

clue.text: General, though belted, was no earl

definitions.text: General, though belted, was no earl

parts.words: General, though belted, was no earl
parts.note: a 'belted earl' is a stock phrase for a peer; this general gave his name to a belt but held no earldom

explanation.surface: A military commander wore a sash yet held no aristocratic title.
explanation.walkthrough: General Sir Samuel Browne devised the officer's belt with a diagonal shoulder strap that bears his name; earls were invested with a sword-belt, hence 'belted earl'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian general lent his name to the officer's waist belt with a supporting strap over the shoulder.

clue.text: Pie-crust inspires him

parts.note: the proverb says promises are like pie-crust, made to be broken, so someone who models himself on pie-crust breaks his word

explanation.surface: A baker is moved to creativity by pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Promises and pie-crust are made to be broken' makes pie-crust the model for someone who fails to keep their word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who goes back on a pledge they have given is described by this compound.

clue.text: Beat the elderly? That's where you come in

parts.note: to thresh is to beat grain from the husks
old people, the aged

explanation.surface: Someone asks about assaulting old people, then points to an entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat the elderly?' reads as an outrageous question, but splits into two plain synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: The sill or strip under a doorway is where one steps on entering a building.

clue.text: The peristeronic epic poet

definitions.meaning: peristeronic means relating to pigeons, so this is the homing kind
the Greek author of the Iliad and the Odyssey

explanation.surface: A pigeon-fancying author of heroic verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peristeronic' is a rare word meaning of pigeons; a homer is a homing pigeon.
explanation.definitionFit: A homing pigeon is called by the same name as the blind bard credited with the Iliad.

clue.text: Valentine's daughterly alternative ?

definitions.meaning: Valentine and his twin brother are heroes of an old French romance; one twin was raised by a bear
a daughter's alternative would be the other kind of child, read as 'or' plus a male child

explanation.surface: Someone muses on a substitute for a daughter on Valentine's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: The medieval romance Valentine and Orson tells of twin brothers parted at birth; split in two, the name is 'or son', the alternative to a daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: The wild twin of the romance is Valentine's brother, and a son is the choice instead of a daughter.

clue.text: One vehicle for him — terrible!

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a van is a road vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a single car for a man is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the Russian tsar known as 'the Terrible'; 'terrible' looks like a comment on the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixteenth-century Russian tsar is remembered by the epithet the Terrible.

clue.text: Takes a beating at the party

definitions.meaning: a percussion instrument that is struck with sticks
an old word for a large evening gathering or tea party

explanation.surface: Someone gets thrashed at a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries a 'drum' was a fashionable evening party, a sense now found mainly in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A percussion instrument is struck repeatedly, and the same word once named a crowded evening reception.

clue.text: Idle chatter of Heather in a distinguished club

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other

parts.note: Pratt's is an exclusive London gentlemen's club
ling is a common heather

explanation.surface: Gossip from a woman named Heather at a smart club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name; it is the plant LING, which goes 'in' PRATT'S, a small exclusive gentlemen's club in St James's, London.
explanation.definitionFit: Childish or foolish talk going on and on is described by this plural noun.

clue.text: Hair-splitting !

parts.note: hair-splitting usually means pedantry, but taken literally it is dividing the hair on the head along a line

explanation.surface: An exclamation at someone's pedantic quibbling.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, splitting the hair is combing it to either side along a line on the scalp.
explanation.definitionFit: The line on the scalp where hair is combed in opposite directions is what the literal reading describes.

clue.text: Funambulist's performances here

parts.note: a funambulist is a tightrope walker, so their acts might seem to happen in the long sheds where cordage is made

explanation.surface: A tightrope artist's shows take place at this venue.
explanation.walkthrough: A rope-walk is a long covered alley where rope is twisted; a funambulist's act is literally a walk on a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Long narrow sheds where strands are laid out and twisted into cordage carry this name.

clue.text: Poor literary productions

parts.note: sounds like bad books, but means hastily written, barely legible handwriting

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses some weak books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary' looks like a reference to literature, but it is meant in the sense of letters written by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Untidy, hurried handwriting is a poor production of written letters.

clue.text: A simple change transfixes

indicators.note: a change to these letters is a rearrangement of them

explanation.surface: A small alteration pierces someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'simple' looks like an adjective on 'change', but 'A simple' is the fodder and 'change' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: To pierce something right through with a sharp point is to skewer or transfix it.

clue.text: No inebriated return ticket from the beach

annotationWithheld.why: No inebriated return ticket from the beach (7): SINGLE ('No return ticket') slurred to SH by 'inebriated', but the indicator splits the one phrase that gives SINGLE, so no leaf can quote it
annotationWithheld.clue: No inebriated return ticket from the beach

clue.text: Put in the soup by a shot at Bert

parts.note: a pot is a shot, as in a potshot or a pot in snooker
Bert is one short form of Herbert; a shot at it, another try at shortening the name, gives the other short form

explanation.surface: Something ends up in the soup thanks to someone taking aim at Bert.
explanation.walkthrough: Herbert shortens to Bert or to Herb, so 'a shot at Bert' is another attempt at Herbert's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: A leafy plant grown for flavouring broth and stews is what goes into the soup pot.

clue.text: Much thought has gone into this statue

definitions.text: Much thought has gone into this statue

parts.words: Much thought has gone into this statue
parts.note: it sounds like praise for a carefully planned sculpture, but means Rodin's famous seated figure deep in contemplation

explanation.surface: Praise for a carefully planned sculpture.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodin's bronze Le Penseur (The Thinker) shows a man lost in thought, so much thought is literally put into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodin's bronze of a seated man chin on hand is known in French by this name, meaning the thinker.

clue.text: Draws towards a Scottish lawyer

parts.note: to means towards
WS is a Writer to the Signet, a Scottish solicitor

explanation.surface: Something pulls in the direction of an Edinburgh solicitor.
explanation.walkthrough: W.S., a Writer to the Signet, is a member of a society of Scottish solicitors.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull a vehicle or boat along behind is to drag or haul it.

clue.text: I'm among draughts, look

indicators.note: one piece goes among, so inside, the letters of the other

parts.note: draughts pieces are called men
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone says they are surrounded by cold air currents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draughts' suggests chilly air, but it is the board game (checkers in the US) whose pieces are men.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's bearing or appearance, their air or expression, is a noun sense of the definition.

clue.text: Ignited by sappers in a measure

parts.note: lit means set alight
RE is the Royal Engineers, whose soldiers are called sappers

explanation.surface: Military engineers set something alight in a controlled way.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers are the British Army's corps of sappers.
explanation.definitionFit: A metric unit of volume is a measure of capacity.

clue.text: "God! I will pack, and take a " (Brooke)

definitions.text: "God! I will pack, and take a " (Brooke)

parts.words: "God! I will pack, and take a " (Brooke)
parts.note: a line from Rupert Brooke's poem The Old Vicarage, Grantchester, where the homesick poet resolves to go back to England by rail

explanation.surface: A quotation from Rupert Brooke with its last word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the missing word from Brooke's Grantchester: the poet in Berlin longs to pack and take the railway home.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet's means of getting home is the railway carriage he plans to board.

clue.text: She is well within my range

indicators.note: the name sits well inside the words that follow, its letters running across them

explanation.surface: A woman is comfortably inside the area I can reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is well within my range' reads as reachable, but the letters of a girl's name run across 'my range'.
explanation.definitionFit: A female name is clued by the pronoun for a woman.

clue.text: Little Miss Trent gets the bird

definitions.meaning: Little Nell Trent is the heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop, a pet form of her name
a giant petrel, a large seabird of southern oceans

explanation.surface: A young lady named Trent is jilted or jeered at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets the bird' sounds like being booed, but is just a link to a second definition: the seabird of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's child heroine Nell Trent has a pet form of her name that is also a name for the giant petrel.

clue.text: Mr. Verdant has returned in the money

parts.note: verdant means green, so Mr Verdant is Mr Green
back means returned, as in come back

explanation.surface: A gentleman called Verdant has come home with a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr. Verdant' looks like a person; it is just the colour, and 'has returned' gives BACK.
explanation.definitionFit: A US dollar bill, printed in green ink on its reverse side, is slang for paper currency.

clue.text: Offender against the body politic

parts.note: the body politic is the nation, so one who offends against it is jailed for political reasons

explanation.surface: A description of a criminal who harms society.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'body politic' is the state, and someone confined for offences against it, such as treason, is held for political crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone imprisoned for political offences such as sedition or treason is the kind of captive meant.
